analysis.investment_thesis: Datamatics is a financially sound IT services business with a decade of unbroken earnings and negligible debt, but at P/E 20.3x and P/B 3.04x it trades at roughly 70% above its Graham Number of ~₹440, offering no margin of safety. The disciplined investor must wait for Mr. Market to offer this business at a sensible price.
key_strengths: 10 consecutive years of positive net profits (₹45 Cr in 2016 → ₹206 Cr in 2025, 18.4% CAGR) — the earnings record Graham demands
Near-debt-free balance sheet: D/E of 0.13 and net cash positive (₹218 Cr cash vs ₹190 Cr total debt in FY2025)
Consistent free cash flow generation — FCF positive all 5 years, rising to ₹201 Cr in FY2025, with OCF/Net Profit ratio of ~1.09 confirming earnings quality
key_risks: Valuation far exceeds intrinsic value: Graham Number ~₹440 vs current price ₹748 — 70% premium with no margin of safety
Borrowings surged from ₹17 Cr (FY2024) to ₹186 Cr (FY2025) — a 10x jump in one year deserves scrutiny on purpose and repayment
Other Income has ballooned to ₹78 Cr (FY2025), representing ~38% of net profit — inflated earnings that may not recur from core operations
red_flags: P/B of 3.04 — more than double my maximum threshold of 1.5; paying excessive premium over tangible assets
Debt spike in FY2025 (₹17 Cr → ₹186 Cr) without clear explanation in available data
FII ownership at 0.48% and DII at 0.11% — near-total institutional absence is a warning signal on liquidity and governance scrutiny
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Datamatics passes the qualitative tests I hold most dear: ten uninterrupted years of earnings, a debt-to-equity of 0.13, interest coverage of roughly 19x (operating income ₹232 Cr vs finance cost ₹12 Cr), and free cash flow that has compounded meaningfully. These are hallmarks of a financially conservative business that would survive an economic downturn — exactly the balance-sheet resilience I require. The net profit CAGR of 18.4% over nine years is admirable and demonstrates genuine operating improvement, not financial engineering.

However, the cardinal rule of value investing is price discipline. At ₹748, the stock trades at P/E 20.3x and P/B 3.04x — both well above my thresholds of 15x and 1.5x respectively. My Graham Number, computed as √(22.5 × EPS ₹34.9 × BVPS ₹246), yields approximately ₹440. The investor who buys at ₹748 is paying a 70% premium to that figure and has absorbed all the optimism of Mr. Market into their cost basis, leaving no cushion against disappointment. Add to this the unexplained tenfold surge in borrowings from ₹17 Cr to ₹186 Cr in a single year, and the growing reliance on Other Income (₹78 Cr, nearly double the prior year) to support net profit, and the prudent investor must exercise patience and await a more reasonable price.
